overview: PySpark reads and writes CSV via spark.read.csv / DataFrameReader.option(...).csv(...) and DataFrame.write.csv(...), controlled by options such as header, inferSchema, sep, quote, escape, nullValue, dateFormat, multiLine, and mode.
Schema handling is a key decision: inferSchema is convenient but triggers an extra full pass over the data to deduce types, whereas supplying an explicit StructType is faster and deterministic.

Malformed-record handling (PERMISSIVE, DROPMALFORMED, FAILFAST) plus the _corrupt_record column governs robustness, and despite its ubiquity CSV is a poor big-data format compared to columnar, splittable Parquet.
learningObjectives: Read and write CSV in PySpark with correct header, separator, quote, escape, nullValue, and dateFormat options.
Understand why inferSchema costs an extra pass and when to provide an explicit schema instead.
Apply parse modes (PERMISSIVE, DROPMALFORMED, FAILFAST) and the _corrupt_record column, and articulate why CSV underperforms Parquet for big data.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: CSV (Comma-Separated Values) support in Spark is provided by the built-in csv data source, which parses delimited text into a DataFrame according to a set of reader options (delimiter, quoting, escaping, null tokens, date/timestamp formats, multiline handling, and a parse mode) and either an inferred or explicitly supplied schema, and serializes a DataFrame back to delimited text on write.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: CSV is a plain text table where each line is a row and commas separate the columns. PySpark can load it into a DataFrame, but it needs hints: is the first line a header? What types are the columns? What character separates fields, and how are commas inside text protected with quotes? You also choose what to do with broken lines. CSV is easy for humans but slow and bulky for big data, so we usually convert it to Parquet.
coreConcept.historicalContext: CSV predates databases as a lingua franca for tabular data exchange, formalized loosely by RFC 4180 in 2005. Spark's CSV support began as the external spark-csv (Databricks) package and was merged into Spark core in version 2.0 (2016) as a first-class data source, gaining richer options and malformed-record handling over subsequent releases.

whyItMatters.business: CSV is the universal interchange format for exports, partner feeds, and legacy systems, so robust ingestion is essential for onboarding external data.
whyItMatters.engineering: Correct option handling (quoting, escaping, multiline, nulls, dates) prevents silent data corruption during ingestion, while parse modes make pipelines fail loudly or skip bad rows by design.
whyItMatters.scalability: CSV is row-oriented and (when uncompressed or gzip-compressed) often not splittable, limiting parallelism; understanding this drives conversion to Parquet for large datasets.
whyItMatters.cost: CSV's lack of compression and columnar pruning inflates storage and scan I/O, raising cloud storage and compute bills compared to Parquet.
whyItMatters.reliability: Explicit schemas and FAILFAST/_corrupt_record handling make ingestion deterministic and surface data quality issues instead of hiding them.

coreComponents.name: DataFrameReader CSV options
coreComponents.definition: Options like header, sep, quote, escape, nullValue, dateFormat, multiLine passed via .option()/.options() to control parsing.
coreComponents.purpose: To correctly interpret delimited text into typed columns.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Define field boundaries, quoting/escaping, null tokens, and date parsing.

coreComponents.name: Schema strategy (inferSchema vs explicit StructType)
coreComponents.definition: Either let Spark deduce column types by scanning the data, or pass a predefined StructType.
coreComponents.purpose: To assign types to columns; explicit schemas avoid an extra pass and ambiguity.
coreComponents.responsibilities: inferSchema does a second full read; explicit schema is single-pass and deterministic.

coreComponents.name: Parse mode and _corrupt_record
coreComponents.definition: mode (PERMISSIVE, DROPMALFORMED, FAILFAST) plus the configurable _corrupt_record column capturing unparseable rows.
coreComponents.purpose: To decide how malformed rows are handled during parsing.
coreComponents.responsibilities: PERMISSIVE keeps bad rows (nulls + corrupt text), DROPMALFORMED discards them, FAILFAST aborts.

internalWorking: On read, Spark lists the input files and creates splits; for splittable inputs (plain uncompressed text without multiLine) it can parallelize across blocks, while gzip or multiLine forces whole-file (non-splittable) reads.
If inferSchema is true, Spark performs an extra job that scans the data to determine column types before the actual read; with an explicit schema this pass is skipped, making startup faster.

During parsing each line is tokenized using sep/quote/escape rules; rows that do not match the schema are routed according to mode: PERMISSIVE nulls the bad fields and (if present) stores the raw line in _corrupt_record, DROPMALFORMED filters them out, and FAILFAST throws an exception.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: CSV files -> File listing & splitting -> (optional) inferSchema scan pass -> Tokenize lines (sep/quote/escape) -> Type cast + mode handling (_corrupt_record) -> DataFrame
dataFlowWalkthrough: 2. Spark lists matching files and computes input splits.
3. Because an explicit schema is provided, no inferSchema pass runs.
4. Each partition reads its lines, tokenizes by comma honoring quotes/escapes, and casts to the schema types.
5. A row that fails to parse has its bad fields nulled and the raw text captured in _corrupt_record (PERMISSIVE), yielding the final DataFrame.

keyTerminology.meaning: A reader option that makes Spark scan the data to deduce column types.
keyTerminology.importance: Convenient but triggers an extra full pass; explicit schemas are preferred in production.

keyTerminology.meaning: A special string column that captures the raw text of rows that failed to parse under PERMISSIVE mode.
keyTerminology.importance: Lets you inspect and quarantine bad records instead of losing them silently; must be declared in the schema to populate.

keyTerminology.meaning: An input file that Spark can divide into independent byte-range splits for parallel reading.
keyTerminology.importance: Plain text is splittable; gzip and multiLine CSV are not, limiting parallelism on large files.

importantConcepts.explanation: With inferSchema=true Spark launches an extra job that reads the full dataset to sample and resolve types before the real read, roughly doubling the I/O at load time. Providing an explicit StructType eliminates this pass.

When you supply an explicit schema and want PERMISSIVE-mode bad rows captured, the schema must include a column named _corrupt_record (or columnNameOfCorruptRecord) of StringType; otherwise the raw bad text is dropped.

quote defines the character wrapping fields that contain the separator; escape defines how a quote inside a quoted field is escaped; multiLine=true allows a single field's quoted value to span multiple physical lines (at the cost of splittability).

variationsAndTypes: **Headered vs headerless CSV:** header=true uses the first line as column names; otherwise Spark assigns _c0, _c1, ...
**Custom-delimited (TSV/PSV):** sep='\t' or sep='|' for tab- or pipe-separated files.
**Quoted/escaped CSV:** quote and escape handle separators and quotes embedded in field values.
**Multiline CSV:** multiLine=true for fields containing embedded newlines (non-splittable).
**Parse modes:** PERMISSIVE (default), DROPMALFORMED, and FAILFAST control malformed-row behavior.
advantages: **Universal interchange:** Readable by virtually every tool and human.
**Simple and text-based:** Easy to generate, diff, and debug.
**No schema embedding required:** Quick to produce from many sources.
**Wide tooling support:** Native data source in Spark with rich options.
disadvantages: **No embedded schema:** Types must be inferred (costly) or supplied externally.
**Row-oriented, no column pruning:** Must read entire rows even for one column.
**Often not splittable:** gzip/multiLine limit parallelism on large files.
**No compression/encoding efficiency:** Larger storage and I/O than columnar formats; no predicate pushdown.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use CSV for data interchange, small/medium files, human inspection, partner feeds, and ingestion landing zones before conversion.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid CSV as a query/storage format for large analytical datasets; convert to Parquet (or ORC/Delta) for columnar pruning, compression, predicate pushdown, and splittability.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: CSV is like a handwritten ledger sheet: anyone can read it, but to find one column you must scan every line, there is no index, and a smudge (malformed line) can confuse the reader. Parquet is like a well-indexed spreadsheet stored by column with summaries, so you can jump straight to what you need.

commonMisconceptions.reality: inferSchema launches an additional full scan of the data to deduce types, roughly doubling read I/O at load time and risking wrong type guesses; explicit schemas are faster and deterministic.

commonMisconceptions.myth: CSV files are always read in parallel like Parquet.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Gzip-compressed CSV and multiLine CSV are not splittable, so each file is read by a single task, severely limiting parallelism on large inputs.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Large gzip or multiLine CSVs read on one task each; split big files, avoid multiLine when possible, or convert to Parquet for parallel, prunable reads.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Use explicit schemas and FAILFAST (or PERMISSIVE with _corrupt_record quarantine) so type/format errors surface deterministically rather than corrupting data silently.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Idempotent reads from immutable CSV landing zones allow safe re-runs; capture bad rows via _corrupt_record for reprocessing.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Track count of _corrupt_record rows and parse failures; alert when malformed-row ratio exceeds a threshold indicating upstream schema drift.
productionConsiderations.security: CSV in object storage should be access-controlled and encrypted; beware CSV-injection in fields and PII in plain text exports.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: CSV's poor compression and full-row scans inflate storage and compute; converting hot datasets to Parquet cuts both storage size and scan cost substantially.
productionConsiderations.performance: Provide explicit schema to skip the infer pass, prune to needed columns after load, and prefer splittable, uncompressed or bzip2/Parquet inputs over gzip for parallelism.

codeExamples.title: Reading CSV with explicit schema and common options
codeExamples.overview: Reads a pipe-separated, headered CSV with an explicit schema (no inferSchema pass), custom null token, and date format.
codeExamples.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
from pyspark.sql.types import StructType, StructField, IntegerType, StringType, DateType, DoubleType

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("csv_read").getOrCreate()

schema = StructType([
    StructField("id", IntegerType(), True),
    StructField("name", StringType(), True),
    StructField("signup_date", DateType(), True),
    StructField("amount", DoubleType(), True),
])

df = (spark.read
    .option("header", True)
    .option("sep", "|")
    .option("quote", "\"")
    .option("escape", "\"")
    .option("nullValue", "NA")
    .option("dateFormat", "yyyy-MM-dd")
    .schema(schema)
    .csv("s3://bucket/customers/*.csv"))

df.printSchema()
df.show(5)
codeExamples.breakdown: An explicit StructType is supplied so Spark skips the inferSchema pass. header=True consumes the first line as column names. sep='|' sets the delimiter, quote/escape handle embedded delimiters/quotes, nullValue='NA' maps the token NA to null, and dateFormat parses signup_date into a DateType.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: A DataFrame with the four typed columns; printSchema shows id:int, name:string, signup_date:date, amount:double, and 'NA' tokens appear as null.
codeExamples.commonIssues: If dateFormat does not match the file's actual format, dates parse to null (PERMISSIVE) or fail (FAILFAST). A wrong sep yields a single _c0 column or merged fields.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Always pass an explicit schema in production to avoid the extra infer scan and to lock types deterministically.

codeExamples.title: Handling malformed rows with parse modes and _corrupt_record
codeExamples.overview: Demonstrates PERMISSIVE capture of bad rows, DROPMALFORMED, and FAILFAST behavior.
codeExamples.code:
from pyspark.sql.types import StructType, StructField, IntegerType, StringType

base = StructType([
    StructField("id", IntegerType(), True),
    StructField("name", StringType(), True),
])

# PERMISSIVE: capture raw bad lines in _corrupt_record (must be in schema)
perm_schema = base.add(StructField("_corrupt_record", StringType(), True))
perm = (spark.read
    .option("header", True)
    .option("mode", "PERMISSIVE")
    .schema(perm_schema)
    .csv("s3://bucket/raw/*.csv"))
bad = perm.filter(F.col("_corrupt_record").isNotNull())

# DROPMALFORMED: silently discard rows that do not match the schema
clean = (spark.read
    .option("header", True)
    .option("mode", "DROPMALFORMED")
    .schema(base)
    .csv("s3://bucket/raw/*.csv"))

# FAILFAST: abort the job on the first malformed row
strict = (spark.read
    .option("header", True)
    .option("mode", "FAILFAST")
    .schema(base)
    .csv("s3://bucket/raw/*.csv"))
codeExamples.breakdown: PERMISSIVE (the default) nulls bad fields and stores the raw line in _corrupt_record, which must be declared in the schema to be populated. DROPMALFORMED filters out rows that do not match the schema. FAILFAST throws an exception on the first malformed row, failing the job loudly.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: perm contains all rows with bad ones flagged via non-null _corrupt_record (filterable into a quarantine 'bad'); clean omits malformed rows; strict raises an exception if any malformed row exists.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting to add _corrupt_record to the schema means PERMISSIVE silently drops the raw bad text. FAILFAST aborts the whole job, so it is best for strict ingestion contracts only.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use PERMISSIVE with a _corrupt_record quarantine table in production so bad rows are inspected and reprocessed, not lost.

codeExamples.title: Writing CSV and converting to Parquet
codeExamples.overview: Writes a DataFrame to CSV with options, then converts the same data to Parquet to show the format upgrade.
codeExamples.code:
# Write CSV with header and a chosen null token
(df.write
    .mode("overwrite")
    .option("header", True)
    .option("sep", ",")
    .option("nullValue", "")
    .csv("s3://bucket/export/customers_csv"))

# Convert to Parquet for efficient analytical storage
(df.write
    .mode("overwrite")
    .parquet("s3://bucket/curated/customers_parquet"))

# Reading back Parquet needs no schema/infer options and prunes columns
fast = spark.read.parquet("s3://bucket/curated/customers_parquet").select("id", "amount")
fast.show(5)
codeExamples.breakdown: Writing CSV emits one part file per output partition with the header in each (header is repeated per file). Converting to Parquet embeds the schema, compresses columnar data, and enables column pruning and predicate pushdown, so reading back only id and amount scans far less data.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: A directory of CSV part files with headers, and a Parquet directory; the Parquet read returns the same data but reads only the selected columns efficiently.
codeExamples.commonIssues: CSV writes the header into every part file. Parquet does not support arbitrary delimiters or human editing, which is the intended tradeoff.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Land raw data as CSV, then immediately convert to partitioned Parquet for all downstream querying to cut I/O and storage.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A company receives daily customer CSV exports from a partner that occasionally contain malformed rows, inconsistent null tokens, and quoted fields with embedded commas. They need a robust ingestion that quarantines bad rows and produces a clean, query-efficient table.
endToEndExample.inputData: Daily pipe-delimited CSV files with a header, 'NULL' as the null token, quoted text fields, and dates formatted MM/dd/yyyy; some rows are truncated or have extra delimiters.
endToEndExample.architecture: PySpark batch job: read CSV from the landing zone with explicit schema + PERMISSIVE + _corrupt_record, split good vs bad rows, write good rows as partitioned Parquet (curated) and bad rows to a quarantine path for review.
processingSteps: 1. Define an explicit StructType including a _corrupt_record StringType column.
2. Read with options header=True, sep='|', quote='"', nullValue='NULL', dateFormat='MM/dd/yyyy', mode='PERMISSIVE'.
3. Split: good = where _corrupt_record is null; bad = where it is not null.
4. Write good rows to curated Parquet partitioned by ingest_date.
5. Write bad rows (raw text) to a quarantine CSV/JSON path for inspection.
6. Emit metrics: total, good, bad counts.
endToEndExample.output: A curated Parquet table of clean, typed customer records and a quarantine dataset of raw malformed lines, plus ingestion quality metrics.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Track the bad-row ratio per batch and alert when it exceeds a threshold (signals upstream schema drift); monitor read parallelism to detect non-splittable gzip inputs.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: PERMISSIVE captures malformed rows in _corrupt_record instead of failing; a separate strict validation job can use FAILFAST on critical feeds where any bad row should halt processing.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Reliable daily ingestion that never silently loses data, surfaces quality issues via quarantine and metrics, and stores clean data as efficient Parquet for fast analytics.

industryUseCases.problem: Ingesting daily CSV exports from external partners with inconsistent formatting and occasional bad rows.
industryUseCases.solution: Explicit-schema CSV reads with PERMISSIVE mode and _corrupt_record quarantine, then conversion to Parquet.
industryUseCases.benefits: Robust ingestion that flags bad rows for review and produces clean, query-efficient curated tables.

industryUseCases.problem: Loading large event CSV dumps that are slow and bulky to query directly.
industryUseCases.solution: Land CSV, immediately convert to partitioned Parquet for analytics with column pruning and predicate pushdown.
industryUseCases.benefits: Drastically reduced scan I/O and storage cost versus querying raw CSV.

industryUseCases.problem: Legacy systems emit headerless, custom-delimited CSV with embedded newlines in free-text fields.
industryUseCases.solution: Read with sep, no-header schema, quote/escape, and multiLine=true; validate and convert downstream.
industryUseCases.benefits: Correct parsing of complex legacy files without data corruption, enabling modern analytics.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Splittability dictates parallelism: plain uncompressed text is splittable, but gzip and multiLine CSVs are read by a single task per file. Split large files, prefer bzip2 or no compression for parallel reads, and convert hot datasets to Parquet for prunable, splittable scans.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Reads from immutable CSV landing zones are idempotent and safely re-runnable. Capturing malformed rows via _corrupt_record enables reprocessing without data loss after fixes.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: As a batch ingestion, HA comes from the cluster manager and durable object storage; deterministic explicit schemas ensure consistent output across retries.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: The raw CSV landing zone is the recovery point; ingestion is reproducible, so curated Parquet can be regenerated by re-running the job against the immutable source.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Always pass an explicit schema to skip the infer pass, avoid multiLine when possible, prefer splittable inputs, project only needed columns after load, and convert to columnar Parquet for repeated querying.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: CSV's full-row scans and weak compression inflate I/O and storage cost; converting to compressed columnar Parquet reduces storage footprint and scan bytes, lowering compute and storage bills.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: CSV exports often contain PII in plain text; encrypt at rest, restrict access, and guard against CSV injection in fields rendered by spreadsheet tools. Avoid logging raw _corrupt_record lines containing sensitive data without masking.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Track parse-failure and _corrupt_record ratios per batch, input file counts, and read parallelism; alert on malformed-ratio spikes (schema drift) and on single-task reads indicating non-splittable inputs.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Validate row counts (input vs good vs quarantined), assert critical columns are non-null after typing, and reconcile parsed totals against source control totals to catch silent parsing errors.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Log good/bad/total counts and schema used per run; alert when bad-row ratio exceeds threshold or when FAILFAST aborts, signaling an upstream contract violation.

recommendedPractices: **Provide an explicit schema** to skip the inferSchema pass and lock types deterministically.
**Use PERMISSIVE with a declared _corrupt_record column** to quarantine bad rows rather than lose them; use FAILFAST for strict contracts.
**Set explicit sep, quote, escape, nullValue, and dateFormat** to match the source exactly and prevent silent corruption.
**Convert raw CSV to Parquet** immediately for any data that will be queried more than once.
engineeringStandards: Production CSV reads must declare an explicit schema; inferSchema is for exploration only.
A parse mode must be set deliberately (default PERMISSIVE), and _corrupt_record must be in the schema when capturing bad rows.
Large CSV inputs must be assessed for splittability; gzip and multiLine require justification.
designRecommendations: Treat CSV as a landing/interchange format, not a query format; curate to Parquet/Delta.
Quarantine malformed rows to a separate path with raw text for reprocessing.
Standardize null tokens and date formats across feeds to simplify ingestion.
namingConventions: Name the corrupt-record column _corrupt_record (the default) unless overridden via columnNameOfCorruptRecord.
Name landing vs curated paths clearly, e.g., /landing/csv and /curated/parquet.
Suffix datasets by format, e.g., customers_csv vs customers_parquet.
documentationStandards: Document the exact reader options (sep, quote, escape, nullValue, dateFormat, mode) per feed.
Document the schema and the chosen parse mode and quarantine strategy.
Record compression and splittability characteristics of source files.
testingStrategies: Unit test parsing on fixtures with embedded delimiters, quotes, nulls, and bad rows for each mode.
Test that _corrupt_record captures malformed lines under PERMISSIVE and that FAILFAST aborts.
Test round-trip CSV write/read and verify counts and types match after Parquet conversion.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: It is the convenient default in tutorials and avoids writing a StructType.
commonMistakes.impact: Triggers an extra full scan (roughly doubling read I/O), can guess wrong types, and is non-deterministic as data changes.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Define an explicit StructType and pass it via .schema(); reserve inferSchema for one-off exploration.

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting _corrupt_record to populate without declaring it.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Developers assume PERMISSIVE always exposes the raw bad text.
commonMistakes.impact: With an explicit schema that omits _corrupt_record, the raw malformed line is dropped and bad rows become invisible.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Add a _corrupt_record StringType column to the schema (or set columnNameOfCorruptRecord) when using PERMISSIVE to capture bad rows.

commonMistakes.mistake: Storing and querying large datasets as gzip CSV.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: CSV is familiar and gzip seems to save space.
commonMistakes.impact: gzip CSV is not splittable so each file is read by one task, crippling parallelism, and row-oriented CSV cannot prune columns or push down predicates, inflating scan cost.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Convert to columnar, splittable Parquet (or Delta/ORC) for any repeatedly queried dataset.

comparisonSection.explanation: CSV is row-oriented text with no embedded schema, weak compression, no column pruning or predicate pushdown, and is often not splittable (gzip/multiLine). Parquet is columnar, compressed, splittable, carries its schema, and supports column pruning and pushdown, making it far cheaper and faster for analytics. Use CSV for interchange, Parquet for querying.

inferSchema launches an extra full scan to deduce types, adding I/O and risking wrong guesses and non-determinism. An explicit schema is single-pass, faster, deterministic, and self-documenting. Prefer explicit schemas in production; use inferSchema only for exploration.

PERMISSIVE keeps bad rows (nulling fields and optionally capturing raw text in _corrupt_record); DROPMALFORMED silently discards them. FAILFAST aborts on the first bad row. Use PERMISSIVE with quarantine for resilient ingestion and FAILFAST for strict data contracts where any bad row must halt the pipeline.

beginnerQuestions.question: How do you read a CSV file with a header into a PySpark DataFrame?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Use spark.read.option('header', True).csv(path), or pass an explicit schema via .schema(my_schema). header=True consumes the first line as column names; otherwise columns are named _c0, _c1, etc.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Mention that without a header or schema Spark uses default _cN names and all string types unless inferSchema is set.

beginnerQuestions.question: What do the header and sep options do?
beginnerQuestions.answer: header tells Spark whether the first line contains column names; sep sets the field delimiter (default comma), e.g., '\t' for TSV or '|' for pipe-separated files.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Tie this to common formats: TSV uses sep='\t', PSV uses sep='|'.

intermediateQuestions.question: Why is inferSchema considered expensive, and what is the alternative?
intermediateQuestions.answer: inferSchema launches an extra job that scans the entire dataset to deduce column types before the real read, roughly doubling load-time I/O, and it can guess types wrong. The alternative is to supply an explicit StructType via .schema(), which is single-pass and deterministic.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Emphasize the two-pass cost and determinism; this is a very common interview question.

intermediateQuestions.question: Explain the CSV parse modes and the role of _corrupt_record.
intermediateQuestions.answer: PERMISSIVE (default) nulls bad fields and stores the raw line in _corrupt_record; DROPMALFORMED discards malformed rows; FAILFAST aborts on the first bad row. _corrupt_record captures the raw text of unparseable rows and must be declared in the schema (or set via columnNameOfCorruptRecord) to populate.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Stress that omitting _corrupt_record from the schema means bad text is silently dropped.

advancedQuestions.question: Why is CSV a poor format for big data compared to Parquet?
advancedQuestions.answer: CSV is row-oriented with no embedded schema, weak/no columnar compression, no column pruning or predicate pushdown, and gzip/multiLine CSVs are not splittable so files are read serially. Parquet is columnar, compressed, splittable, schema-carrying, and supports pruning and pushdown, drastically reducing scan I/O and storage cost.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Hit splittability, columnar pruning, compression, and pushdown explicitly.

advancedQuestions.question: How do quote, escape, and multiLine interact when parsing complex CSV?
advancedQuestions.answer: quote is the character wrapping fields that contain the separator (default '"'); escape is how a quote inside a quoted field is escaped (default '\' in Spark, often set to '"' for RFC 4180 doubled quotes); multiLine=true lets a single quoted field span multiple physical lines. multiLine makes the file non-splittable.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Note the splittability tradeoff of multiLine and the doubled-quote convention.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: A partner CSV feed sometimes has rows with extra delimiters; the pipeline silently loses those rows and analysts complain about missing data. How do you fix it?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Recognize DROPMALFORMED or a schema lacking _corrupt_record is silently dropping bad rows. Decide bad rows must be visible and quarantined.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Switch to PERMISSIVE mode, add a _corrupt_record StringType column to the explicit schema, split rows where _corrupt_record is not null into a quarantine path, and emit a bad-row metric so issues are surfaced rather than lost.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design an ingestion pipeline for daily multi-gigabyte CSV partner feeds that must be query-efficient and resilient to bad data.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Land raw CSV in an immutable zone. Read with explicit schema + PERMISSIVE + _corrupt_record; split good vs bad; write good rows to partitioned Parquet (by date) and bad rows to quarantine. Emit quality metrics.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: PERMISSIVE preserves resilience but needs quarantine handling; FAILFAST is stricter but halts on any bad row. gzip CSV limits parallelism, so prefer splittable inputs or split large files before reading.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Avoid non-splittable gzip/multiLine for large files; convert to Parquet for downstream querying; partition curated data by ingest date and size files to avoid small-file problems.

How do you change the corrupt-record column name?
What happens to dateFormat mismatches under PERMISSIVE vs FAILFAST?
Why is gzip CSV not splittable but bzip2 is?
How does CSV write handle the header across multiple part files?

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: PySpark's CSV data source reads/writes delimited text via options (header, sep, quote, escape, nullValue, dateFormat, multiLine, mode); prefer explicit schemas over inferSchema and convert to Parquet for big-data querying.
keyConcepts: header / sep / quote / escape / nullValue / dateFormat control parsing.
inferSchema = extra full scan; explicit StructType = single-pass, deterministic.
_corrupt_record captures bad rows (must be in schema).
CSV is row-oriented, often non-splittable; Parquet is columnar and far better for analytics.
interviewPoints: inferSchema does an extra full pass; use explicit schema in prod.
_corrupt_record must be declared in the schema to populate.
gzip/multiLine CSV is not splittable, limiting parallelism.
CSV vs Parquet: columnar, compressed, splittable, pushdown.
quickNotes: Without header or schema, columns are _c0, _c1, ... and may be all strings.
Spark's default escape is backslash; set escape='"' for RFC 4180 doubled quotes.
CSV write repeats the header in every part file.
multiLine=true allows embedded newlines but makes files non-splittable.
Land as CSV, curate to partitioned Parquet for all repeated querying.

keyTakeaways: CSV reading is controlled by options (header, sep, quote, escape, nullValue, dateFormat, multiLine, mode); set them explicitly to match the source and prevent silent corruption.
inferSchema triggers an extra full scan of the data to deduce types, so production pipelines should pass an explicit StructType for speed and determinism.
Parse modes (PERMISSIVE, DROPMALFORMED, FAILFAST) plus the _corrupt_record column govern malformed-row handling; _corrupt_record must be declared in the schema to capture bad rows.
gzip and multiLine CSVs are not splittable, so large files are read serially, limiting parallelism; split files or avoid these where parallel reads matter.
CSV is a fine interchange/landing format but a poor query/storage format; convert to columnar, compressed, splittable Parquet for efficient, low-cost analytics.
